summary: Draft Control Power record. `AllowSystemRequiredPowerRequests` sits under `HKLM\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Power`, has an explicit repo-doc default of `1`, is absent on the observed clean baseline, produced an exact current-build Unicode string hit in `ntoskrnl.exe`, and was later retained by source-enrichment as a docs-first kernel candidate with a `power-request-simulation` trigger recommendation. A later repo-native follow-up then exposed that same trigger family as a named guest Procmon profile and mega-trigger runtime alias. A later Microsoft power-setting page plus the companion `Power.admx` / `Power.adml` mapping then documented the public hidden `Allow system required requests` setting family, its `SYSTEMREQUIRED` alias, GUID `a4b195f5-8225-47d8-8012-9d41369786e2`, and `0/1` accepted semantics. A later KVM local-KD pass then resolved live current-build `nt!PopPowerRequestConvertSystemToExecution = 1`, which aligns with the repo-doc default. A later static INIT-table follow-up then showed a current-build `ntoskrnl.exe` descriptor entry under `Power` that binds `AllowSystemRequiredPowerRequests` to the exact global later resolved by local KD as `nt!PopPowerRequestConvertSystemToExecution`. A later current-build disassembly pass then showed direct consumers in `nt!PopPowerRequestHandleExecutionEnablementUpdate` and `nt!PopPowerRequestCallbackExecutionRequired`. Later follow-ups then showed `nt!PopUmpoSendPowerRequestOverrideQuery` packaging requester state for `nt!PopUmpoSendPowerMessage`, `nt!PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredSettingCallback` staying timeout-setting specific by updating `nt!PopExecutionRequiredTimeout`, the timeout timer/worker chain feeding back into `nt!PopPowerRequestHandleExecutionEnablementUpdate`, the broader override-response plus callback-worker path staying queue and PDC driven with no visible `*PowerRequest*Reg*` symbol, and a generic power-setting callback subsystem around `PoRegisterPowerSettingCallback` and `PopInitializePowerSettingCallbacks`. A later host-side objdump follow-up then showed an unlabeled current-build `INIT` walker at `0x140C48AB8` uniquely consuming the broader `Power` descriptor table, passing row key and value names through subkey and value-lookup helpers before copying payload into the paired target global. The lane is strong enough for a schema-backed draft, but Microsoft still does not publish the internal `Control\\Power\\AllowSystemRequiredPowerRequests` seeding path and an exact runtime registry read remains unresolved.

setting.name: Allow System Required Power Requests
setting.casual_explanation: This appears to be a kernel-adjacent Control Power setting tied to how the power manager treats system-required power requests. It is being tracked as a research candidate, not a user-facing tweak.
setting.why_people_change_it: Kernel and power researchers may inspect this value when investigating how system-required power requests are converted, honored, or suppressed under undocumented power-policy flows.
setting.tradeoffs_overview: The value now has a stronger evidence chain because it has repo docs, observed baseline state, an exact current-build string hit, a retained enrichment recommendation, a repo-native trigger harness, Microsoft documentation for the public hidden system-required setting family, a live current-build KVM local-KD value that matches the repo-doc default, direct current-build consumer disassembly, a visible UMPO override-query lineage, a timeout-setting callback disassembly, a retained timeout timer/worker chain, a retained override-response plus callback-worker follow-up that still exposed no visible `*PowerRequest*Reg*` symbol, a retained generic power-setting callback infrastructure pass around `PoRegisterPowerSettingCallback`, and a later host-side static walker analysis that materially closes the old seeding-path gap. It is still too weak for a published tweak because Microsoft does not publish the internal `Control\\Power` seeding path, that path is still statically inferred from current-build analysis, and an exact runtime registry read remains unresolved.
setting.professional_notes: Repo power docs assign `AllowSystemRequiredPowerRequests = 1` under `Control\\Power` and map it to `PopPowerRequestConvertSystemToExecution`. The power routing note later kept the value inside the `Control\\Power` docs cluster. The observed clean baseline then confirmed that the parent `Control\\Power` path exists while the value itself is absent. A later targeted current-build string batch found an exact Unicode hit for `AllowSystemRequiredPowerRequests` in `ntoskrnl.exe`, which is stronger than a pure docs-only mention and enough to keep the value out of raw backlog. Source-enrichment later retained the candidate in the canonical queue with `power-request-simulation` as the suggested trigger family, specifically `PowerCreateRequest(SystemRequired)`, `PowerSetRequest(DisplayRequired)`, and an audio playback session. A later repo-native follow-up then exposed that same trigger family as a named guest Procmon profile plus a matching mega-trigger runtime alias, closing the old trigger-design gap before the first dedicated narrow replay. Microsoft later documented the public hidden `Allow system required requests` power setting, exposing alias `SYSTEMREQUIRED`, GUID `a4b195f5-8225-47d8-8012-9d41369786e2`, and `0/1` accepted semantics, while the local `Power.admx` / `Power.adml` pair corroborated the same family through `AllowSystemPowerRequestAC/DC` policy mappings. A later KVM local-KD pass then resolved live current-build `nt!PopPowerRequestConvertSystemToExecution = 1`, which matches the repo-doc default and also surfaced the sibling symbol `nt!PopPowerRequestActiveAudioEnablesExecutionRequired` in the same wildcard sweep. A later static INIT-table follow-up then found the exact current-build value-name string in `ntoskrnl.exe`, placed it inside an `INIT` descriptor slice under the shared `Power` key string, and matched the paired target-global pointer to `nt!PopPowerRequestConvertSystemToExecution` via the retained local-KD symbol address. A later current-build disassembly pass then showed direct reads of `nt!PopPowerRequestConvertSystemToExecution` inside `nt!PopPowerRequestHandleExecutionEnablementUpdate` and `nt!PopPowerRequestCallbackExecutionRequired`, while `nt!PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredSettingCallback` chained into that same reader family through `PopPowerRequestHandleExecutionmentUpdate`. A later wildcard lineage pass then showed that the current build exposes only one `*PowerRequest*Setting*` symbol, `nt!PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredSettingCallback`, alongside `PopPowerRequestInitialize`, `PopPowerRequestOverrideInitialize`, and the `PopExecutionRequiredTimeout` family. A later init/override disassembly pass then showed `PopPowerRequestInitialize` only zeroing per-object fields and `PopPowerRequestOverrideInitialize` iterating `PopPowerRequestObjectList` before calling `PopUmpoSendPowerRequestOverrideQuery`, which is useful because it still did not expose a registry read in the visible current-build init path. A later dedicated UMPO disassembly pass then showed `PopUmpoSendPowerRequestOverrideQuery` storing requester identity via `PoStoreRequester`, allocating an `Umpo`-tagged buffer, and dispatching `PopUmpoSendPowerMessage`, while wildcard output exposed `PopUmpoSendPowerRequestCreate`, `PopUmpoSendPowerRequestAction`, and `PopUmpoSendPowerRequestOverrideCleanup`. A later dedicated callback disassembly pass then showed `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredSettingCallback` comparing the incoming GUID against `GUID_EXECUTION_REQUIRED_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, requiring a 4-byte payload, writing `PopExecutionRequiredTimeout`, rearming `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredTimeoutTimer`, and then calling `PopPowerRequestHandleExecutionEnablementUpdate`. A later timeout-lineage pass then showed `PopPowerRequestSetExecutionRequiredTimeoutTimer` reading `PopExecutionRequiredTimeout`, comparing it against `PopExecutionRequiredContext`, and arming `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredTimeoutTimer` via `KeSetTimer2`, while `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredTimeoutCallback` simply queued work and `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredTimeoutWorker` re-entered `PopPowerRequestHandleExecutionEnablementUpdate`. A later response-lineage follow-up then showed `x nt!*PowerRequest*Reg*` returning no visible current-build symbols, `PopPowerRequestHandleRequestOverrideQueryResponse` updating request state, re-evaluating pending request status, and queueing `PopPowerRequestUpdateWorkItem`, `PopPowerRequestCallbackWorker` draining the update queue through `PopPowerRequestStatsSetActive` and `PopPowerRequestHandleRequestUpdate`, and `PopPowerRequestCallbackExecutionRequired` consulting `PoPdcCallbacks`, updating `PopPowerRequestPdcNotifiedExecutionRequired` or `PopPowerRequestPdcNotifiedSystemRequired`, testing `PopPowerRequestConvertSystemToExecution`, and then writing `PopSIdle` policy state before `PopCheckResiliencyScenarios`. A later power-setting lineage pass then exposed the broader current-build infrastructure around this family: `x nt!*PowerSetting*` returned `PopInitializePowerSettingCallbacks`, `PopInitializePowerSettings`, `PoRegisterPowerSettingCallback`, `PoUnregisterPowerSettingCallback`, `PopDispatchPowerSettingCallbacks`, `PopCallPowerSettingCallback`, `PopQueryPowerSettingUlong`, `PopSetPowerSettingValue`, and `PopRegisteredPowerSettingCallbacks`, while `x nt!*ExecutionRequired*Setting*` still returned only `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredSettingCallback`. The same pass showed `PoRegisterPowerSettingCallback` allocating a callback object, copying the target GUID and callback pointer, and resolving the setting through `PopFindPowerSettingConfiguration`, which is strong proof that the visible execution-required family now sits on a generic power-setting callback subsystem even though the exact binding site for `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredSettingCallback` is still unresolved. This matters because the visible family is now callback/init/timeout-setting/timer-worker/UMPO/override-response/PDC/power-setting-subsystem driven and still does not demonstrate a registry read or a direct write to `PopPowerRequestConvertSystemToExecution`. A later host-side objdump/xref follow-up then narrowed the old seeding gap substantially: an unlabeled `INIT` walker at `0x140C48AB8` uniquely loads the broader `0x140C72E30` `Power` descriptor table, passes each row key string through `0x1407E334C`, each row value name through `0x14086A794` and `0x14086C510`, and the row target pointer through `0x140C4CB20`; this is best read as the current-build static registry seeding path for the execution-required pair even though the routine is not yet symbol-resolved or tied to a Microsoft publication of the internal `Control\\Power` seeding path. A 2026-04-12 QGA-launched WPR boot-registry attempt then armed and collected the boot trace successfully, generated a 1.55 GB ETL and 2.97 GB tracerpt CSV, and produced a tiny hit CSV containing only the header: no exact `AllowSystemRequiredPowerRequests` registry hit appeared. The same run filled the guest trace workspace enough that summary and normalized JSON writes became zero-byte files, so the trace was salvaged via QGA `guest-file-read` and the temporary WPR directories were deleted from the guest. The next proof step remains narrower: symbol-resolve or document the unlabeled init walker, or capture an exact runtime registry read in a smaller/streamed trace lane.

decision.why: The candidate is now stronger than a raw draft because it has repo-doc semantics, observed baseline state, a current-build string hit, a retained enrichment recommendation, a matching repo-native trigger harness, Microsoft documentation for the public hidden system-required setting family, a live KVM local-KD value that aligns with the repo-doc default, direct current-build callback/reader disassembly, a retained Ghidra reader-family corroboration, a retained soft-reboot ETW attempt, a visible UMPO override-query lineage, a timeout-setting callback disassembly, a retained timeout timer/worker chain, a retained override-response plus callback-worker follow-up that still exposed no visible `*PowerRequest*Reg*` symbol, a retained generic power-setting callback subsystem pass around `PoRegisterPowerSettingCallback`, a later current-build INIT-table binding that maps the exact value name to the KD-resolved target global, and a later host-side disassembly follow-up that statically recovers the generic init walker feeding that table.
